structured.recommendation: Adopt progressive delivery (canary) with automated, metric-gated rollback rather than an all-at-once or purely manual staged rollout. Canary directly serves the stated goal of reducing deployment risk (issue:L1) by limiting blast radius to a small traffic slice before full exposure, while preserving delivery speed (issue:L2) because promotion is automatic when health metrics stay green — no human gate slows the common success path. This balances both sides of the question (issue:L3): risk is bounded by exposure percentage and fast rollback, speed is retained by automation rather than manual approvals. Concretely: 1–5% canary → automated SLO/error-rate check → progressive ramp → auto-rollback on breach. This is a recommendation only; council completion does not authorize implementation.

evidence.claim: Primary objective is to reduce deployment risk, which canary addresses by bounding blast radius
Delivery speed must be preserved, which favors automated promotion over manual gates
The question asks which single rollout policy balances risk and speed, inviting a concrete policy proposal
Progressive delivery with automated rollback is a standard pattern for trading blast radius against release velocity

assumptions.statement: The deployment target can serve two versions simultaneously and split traffic by percentage.
assumptions.if_false_then: Canary is infeasible; fall back to blue-green or staged environment rollout, changing the recommendation.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Confirm the runtime/platform (load balancer, service mesh, or platform routing) supports weighted traffic splitting.

assumptions.statement: Health/error-rate/latency signals exist and are reliable enough to gate automated promotion and rollback.
assumptions.if_false_then: Automation gates cannot be trusted; policy degrades to manual canary, reducing the speed benefit.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Inventory existing SLO metrics and their per-version attribution.

assumptions.statement: Rolling back a canary is fast and low-cost (no irreversible migrations at canary stage).
assumptions.if_false_then: Stateful/migration changes need expand-contract handling layered on top of the canary policy.
assumptions.how_to_verify: Check whether releases include schema or data migrations.

risks: Issue provides no deployment frequency, failure rate, or topology, so the recommended canary parameters (percent, bake time) are unvalidated defaults.
Canary adds pipeline and observability complexity that may not pay off for low-frequency or low-blast-radius services.
Automated rollback can mask a flaky metric as a real failure, causing thrash if gates are poorly tuned.
Stateful releases (DB migrations) are not addressed by canary alone and could reintroduce risk.
what_would_change_my_view: Evidence that the platform cannot split traffic, which would shift me toward blue-green.
Data showing very low deployment frequency or trivial blast radius, where canary overhead outweighs benefit and staged manual rollout suffices.
Evidence that releases are dominated by irreversible data migrations, making expand-contract the primary lever rather than traffic-based canary.
structured.next_action: Confirm whether the deployment platform supports weighted traffic splitting and has per-version SLO metrics; if yes, draft a canary policy spec with concrete ramp steps and gate thresholds.
